connection: ClockEntry exists and can be completed. No production component stores more than one entry yet. Create the first in-memory ClockEntryRepository using a private List<ClockEntry> required for saving and retrieving entries.
objectives: Identify ClockEntryRepository's real, public _clockEntries field and explain what capability that exposes to any caller, not just the repository's own methods.
Trace how SaveClockEntry (Add) and GetEmployeeClockEntries (Where, a LINQ extension method on IEnumerable<T>) both operate on the same underlying List<ClockEntry>.
Explain why List<T> was chosen here over an array: the repository does not know how many entries it will ever hold.
Enumerate _clockEntries with foreach and explain what a foreach loop actually calls behind the syntax.

visuals.title: List<ClockEntry> grows as ClockIn is called
visuals.explanation: Every ClockIn call adds one more ClockEntry to _clockEntries -- the list's size is never fixed in advance.

visuals.title: Add appends; Where filters without removing
visuals.explanation: SaveClockEntry calls _clockEntries.Add(entry); GetEmployeeClockEntries calls _clockEntries.Where(...), which reads the list without changing it.

visuals.title: public means any caller can bypass the repository's methods
visuals.explanation: Because _clockEntries is a public field, code outside ClockEntryRepository could call _clockEntries.Clear() or .Add(...) directly, skipping SaveClockEntry entirely -- a real, unfixed encapsulation gap.

visuals.title: foreach is syntax over an enumerator
visuals.explanation: The real leftover foreach(var clockentry in _clockEntries) { } in GetClockEntry compiles to repeated calls to an enumerator's MoveNext/Current, even though this particular loop body does nothing with each element.

preQuiz.prompt: Why does ClockEntryRepository use List<ClockEntry> instead of ClockEntry[]?
options: The repository has no way to know how many entries it will ever hold -- List<T> grows as SaveClockEntry adds more, which a fixed-size array cannot do without manual resizing
List<T> is required by the IClockEntryRepository interface
preQuiz.explanation: An array's length is fixed at creation; a growing collection of unknown final size is exactly what List<T> is for.

preQuiz.prompt: What does _clockEntries being a public field (not private) actually expose to code outside ClockEntryRepository?
options: Direct access to Add, Remove, Clear, and every other List<ClockEntry> member -- completely bypassing SaveClockEntry and any future validation it might contain
Nothing extra -- public fields behave identically to private ones
Only read access, never write access
preQuiz.explanation: A public field grants full read/write access to the underlying list's entire API, not just the repository's intended SaveClockEntry/GetEmployeeClockEntries/GetClockEntry surface.

preQuiz.prompt: What does the real, leftover foreach(var clockentry in _clockEntries) { } inside GetClockEntry actually do?
options: It enumerates every entry and does nothing with each one -- a genuine, harmless-but-pointless leftover in the production code, kept intentionally as a 'spot the smell' artifact
It searches for the requested employeeId
preQuiz.explanation: The loop body is empty in the learner solution -- confirmed by reading Repositories/ClockEntryRepository.cs directly. It has no effect on the method's behavior.

concept.title: List<ClockEntry> is the repository's only storage
paragraphs: Create this temporary implementation in the Domain project's Repositories folder: src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain/Repositories/ClockEntryRepository.cs. Keep its namespace as PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain; a folder helps organize files but does not have to change the namespace.

This placement is curriculum scaffolding, not a rule that concrete repositories belong in Domain. Session 11 is isolating List<T> and in-memory storage before the course introduces infrastructure boundaries. A finished architecture normally keeps the repository contract with the code that depends on it and places database or other external storage implementations in Infrastructure.

_clockEntries is declared public readonly List<ClockEntry> _clockEntries = new(); -- readonly means the field itself can never be reassigned to point at a different list, but the list's contents remain fully mutable through Add, Remove, Clear, and indexing.
Every real method on ClockEntryRepository -- SaveClockEntry, GetClockEntry, GetEmployeeClockEntries -- reads or writes this one list. There is no other storage anywhere in the class.
concept.code:
// Repositories/ClockEntryRepository.cs -- the real, complete storage
public readonly List<ClockEntry> _clockEntries = new();

concept.title: Add and Where operate on the same list, for different purposes
paragraphs: SaveClockEntry's _clockEntries.Add(clockEntry) is List<T>'s own instance method -- it mutates the list in place, growing its Count by one.

GetEmployeeClockEntries's _clockEntries.Where(...) is a LINQ extension method available on any IEnumerable<T>, including List<T> -- it does not mutate anything; it returns a new, deferred query over the existing elements (Session 23).

concept.title: A public field is a real, named smell, not a rewrite target today
paragraphs: This session names the problem without fixing it: nothing stops calling code from writing repository._clockEntries.Clear() directly, deleting every clock entry without going through any method at all.
Session 17 (Encapsulation and Composition) is where this gets revisited as an explicit before/after -- this session's job is only to make sure you can see the gap clearly first.
concept.code:
// Legal today, and a real problem -- nothing in ClockEntryRepository prevents this
repository._clockEntries.Clear();

lab.objective: Create the first in-memory ClockEntryRepository using a private List<ClockEntry> required for saving and retrieving entries.
lab.startingCondition: ClockEntry exists and can be completed. No production component stores more than one entry yet.
steps: Create a Repositories folder in the Domain project, then create ClockEntryRepository.cs inside it with the PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain namespace and a private List<ClockEntry>.
Add Save to append an entry.
Add methods to retrieve an employee's entries and locate an open entry.
Update App to save open and completed entries and display the resulting count.
Keep the list private; callers interact through repository behavior.
lab.expectedBehavior: Production stores and retrieves clock entries through behavior rather than exposing its List.
lab.validation: dotnet build PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release && dotnet test PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release --no-build

commit: session-10: teach arrays lists and enumeration
review: The lab uses production because that is the most natural environment for this concept.
Every referenced application artifact was created in this session or an earlier session.
Earlier production code, tests, and ScratchPad experiments remain intact.

postQuiz.prompt: If _clockEntries were changed from List<ClockEntry> to ClockEntry[], what would break first?
options: SaveClockEntry's _clockEntries.Add(...) call -- arrays have no Add method; a fixed-size array cannot grow to accept new entries
GetEmployeeClockEntries's Where call -- arrays do not support LINQ
Nothing -- arrays and List<T> are interchangeable everywhere
postQuiz.explanation: Arrays support LINQ's Where perfectly well (they implement IEnumerable<T>), but they have no Add method -- List<T>'s growable capacity is specifically what SaveClockEntry depends on.

postQuiz.prompt: What is the real, concrete risk of _clockEntries being public, beyond 'it looks untidy'?
options: Any code anywhere in the same process that has a ClockEntryRepository reference can mutate its stored entries directly, bypassing whatever business rules SaveClockEntry might someday enforce
Public fields cause a measurable performance penalty
It prevents the repository from implementing IClockEntryRepository
postQuiz.explanation: The real risk is behavioral: any future validation added to SaveClockEntry can be silently bypassed by code that mutates _clockEntries directly instead.

postQuiz.prompt: Does GetEmployeeClockEntries's Where call remove non-matching entries from _clockEntries?
options: No -- Where returns a new filtered view without modifying the underlying list at all; _clockEntries still contains every entry afterward
Yes -- Where permanently removes entries that do not match
Only entries where ClockOut is null are removed
postQuiz.explanation: LINQ's Where is non-destructive by design -- this is part of why Session 23's deferred-execution discussion matters: querying never mutates the source.

reflections.question: Why does this session deliberately not fix the public-field problem it identifies -- what would you lose by fixing it here instead of in Session 17?
reflections.answer: Session 11 is isolating how List<T> storage and mutation work. Fixing encapsulation at the same time would mix that learning goal with access design and hide the concrete problem before the learner has observed it. Preserving the flaw gives Session 17 a motivated before-and-after refactor rather than an abstract rule.

reflections.question: What would you need to add to ClockEntryRepository to make _clockEntries.Add(...) impossible from outside the class, while keeping SaveClockEntry's own behavior unchanged?
reflections.answer: Make the mutable list field private, for example private readonly List<ClockEntry> _clockEntries = new();. SaveClockEntry can continue calling _clockEntries.Add internally. External code should receive only purpose-specific methods or a read-only view when it genuinely needs to inspect entries.

reflections.question: Where else in this codebase might a similarly 'too-permissive' field or property be hiding?
reflections.answer: Good candidates to audit include publicly exposed collections and settable model properties such as Employee.Name or Employee.Address. The question is whether callers truly need unrestricted replacement or mutation. A public setter is not automatically wrong, but it should correspond to an intentional operation rather than convenience alone.

whatBreaks: Directly clearing or mutating _clockEntries from outside ClockEntryRepository bypasses SaveClockEntry entirely, and would silently corrupt GetClockEntry/GetEmployeeClockEntries's results for any code that assumed only SaveClockEntry could add entries. Replacing List<ClockEntry> with a fixed-size array would break SaveClockEntry's Add call the moment more entries are saved than the array's original length allows.
summary: List<ClockEntry> is ClockEntryRepository's entire storage: SaveClockEntry mutates it with Add, while GetEmployeeClockEntries and GetClockEntry read it with LINQ's Where and FirstOrDefault without changing it. The field's real public accessibility is a genuine, currently-unfixed encapsulation gap -- named honestly here, and revisited as an explicit fix in Session 17.
